content: Full-text articles were retrieved for all studies identified as potentially eligible after the initial screening phase. Data extraction was conducted using a piloted data extraction form to determine study inclusion. The first section of the form contained information necessary to decide on inclusion. If a study was deemed ineligible, the remaining sections of the form were not completed. For studies that were included, the second section of the form was completed. Data extracted included study details (location, year, contextual information), methods (study design, duration, setting, risk of bias, withdrawals, and study period), participants (number, age, gender, diagnostic criteria, inclusion/exclusion criteria), exposure and comparison details (description, duration, intensity, content, co-exposures), outcomes (specified outcomes, time points of measurement), and other information (funding sources, conflicts of interest). The risk of bias (RoB) and other quality features of each study were assessed to create an evidence profile. RoB checklists were selected based on study design, and the results of these assessments are presented in Appendix 20. Evidence was synthesized narratively, and evidence summaries and standard summary of findings tables were prepared for presentation to the guideline development group (GDG). The search results included 20 studies: six interventional studies (five randomized trials and one pre-post design) and 14 observational studies (six cohort studies, seven case-control studies, and one retrospective analysis of cross-sectional data). All five randomized trials were conducted in high-income countries, while the pre-post interventional study was from rural India. Most observational studies were also from high-income countries, with three conducted in lowand middle-income countries (Bangladesh, Iran, and Iraq). Further details of the included studies are provided in Appendix 19. The studies included a range of participants, such as children under five, older children, caregivers, community-dwelling older adults, visually impaired older adults, emergency department patients, and burn registry patients. One study specifically recruited visually impaired adults over 75 years old, while none targeted differently-abled individuals living in the community. The review examined several interventions and exposures, including fire/smoke alarms, carbon monoxide detectors, stairway safety gates, window guards, fireguards, unvented gas stoves, and home safety assessment/modification programs. Evidence on the effectiveness of these interventions varied. For example, properly installed and functioning smoke alarms were found to reduce burn injuries. Randomized trials and case-control studies supported the role of smoke alarms in preventing burns and fires, though some studies reported mixed results regarding their usage rates among burn cases. Stair safety gates were associated with reduced hospital admissions and emergency visits for children under five. Window guards were found to be effective in preventing falls, as demonstrated by a cross-sectional study in the USA. Home safety assessment and modification programs showed mixed results, with some randomized trials reporting reductions in falls and medically attended injuries, while others found no significant effects. A dose-response relationship was observed between the number of home hazards and the likelihood of injuries requiring medical attention. For instance, a New Zealand study estimated a 22% increase in injury odds with each additional home hazard. Similarly, a Canadian study found that an increase in home hazards was associated with a higher risk of fall-related medical visits among older adults. Supplementary evidence from individual studies and related systematic reviews was also identified. For example, Johnston (2011) highlighted design parameters associated with window falls, while Clouatre (2013) and Phillips (2011) examined the impact of anti-scalding interventions. However, no quality appraisal was conducted for these supplementary studies. In summary, the evidence base for home safety modifications and their impact on health outcomes is limited by the lack of high-quality studies. While some interventions, such as smoke alarms and home safety programs, show promise, the overall evidence is inconsistent. Most studies were conducted in high-income countries, with limited data from low-income settings. The findings emphasize the importance of maintaining functional smoke alarms and implementing targeted safety interventions to reduce injury risks.
